notes.17:18: Latin seminiverbius (literally "word-sower") renders Greek spermologos ("seed-picker" or "babbler"); the Vulgate also reads novorum daemoniorum ("new divinities") where Greek has "foreign divinities."
notes.17:22: Latin superstitiosiores ("quite/more superstitious"), softened by quasi ("as it were"), renders Greek deisidaimonesterous, which can be understood either positively ("very religious") or critically ("very superstitious").
notes.17:30: The Vulgate reads hujus ignorantiae ("of this ignorance") and annuntiat ("proclaims/declares"), where Greek lacks "this" and reads "commands."
notes.18:4: The Vulgate includes interponens nomen Domini Jesu ("introducing the name of the Lord Jesus"), a Western-text addition absent from most Greek manuscripts.
notes.18:7: The Vulgate reads nomine Titi Justi ("named Titus Justus"), preserving the name Titus where Greek manuscripts vary between "Titius Justus" and "Justus."
notes.18:18: The subject of qui sibi totonderat ("having shaved his head") is grammatically ambiguous between Paul and Aquila, though the Clementine punctuation places Priscilla and Aquila in parentheses to link the clause back to Paul.
notes.18:26: The Vulgate reads fiducialiter agere (literally "to act boldly") and viam Domini ("the way of the Lord"), where Greek manuscripts read "to speak boldly" and "the way of God."
notes.18:27: The Vulgate ends with his qui crediderant ("to those who had believed"), omitting the phrase "through grace" present in Greek manuscripts.
notes.19:9: The Clementine Vulgate reads "the way of the Lord" (viam Domini, also in 19:23, where Greek has simply "the Way") and prints lowercase tyranni cujusdam ("a certain tyrant"), rendering the Greek personal name Tyrannus as a common noun.
notes.19:16: Latin dominatus amborum ("overpowering both of them") literally refers to "both" despite the seven sons mentioned in 19:14, reflecting a reading shared with early Greek witnesses where the term for "both" was sometimes used of more than two.
notes.19:24: Throughout this episode (vv. 24, 27, 28, 34, 35), the Vulgate uses the Roman goddess name Diana rather than the Greek name Artemis.
notes.19:35: Vulgate-distinct reading: cultricem ("worshiper") and Jovisque prolis ("and of the offspring of Jupiter," using the Roman name Jupiter for Zeus) differ from the Greek terms "temple keeper" and "fallen from Zeus/heaven."
notes.19:40: The Vulgate renders the clause personally as nullus obnoxius ("no one guilty") rather than neuter ("no cause"), and follows the Clementine versification that combines Greek verses 40 and 41 into a single verse 40.
notes.20:22: The Latin ablative spiritu ("in spirit," lowercase in the Vulgate) is variously understood as referring either to Paul's own spirit or to the Holy Spirit compelling him (compare Spiritus Sanctus in 20:23).
notes.20:24: The Clementine Vulgate preserves three distinctive readings here: nihil horum vereor ("I fear none of these things"), the comparative pretiosiorem quam me ("more precious than myself," where Greek reads "dear to myself"), and ministerium verbi ("ministry of the word," where Greek reads simply "the ministry").
notes.20:28: Latin episcopos literally means "overseers" or "bishops." The Vulgate renders the following verb as regere ("to govern" or "to rule"), whereas the Greek has "to shepherd," and reads ecclesiam Dei ("the church of God").
notes.20:32: Because Latin qui ("who") is masculine, it refers unambiguously to God (Deo) rather than to the neuter word (verbo), whereas the corresponding Greek participle is grammatically ambiguous.
notes.20:33: The Clementine Vulgate includes sicut ("just as") at the end of verse 33, linking it directly to ipsi scitis ("you yourselves know") at the start of verse 34, whereas Greek editions lack "just as" and begin a new sentence at verse 34.
notes.21:3: Vulgate 'Cum apparuissemus autem Cypro' literally reads 'when we had appeared to Cyprus,' a nautical idiom for coming into view of land, corresponding to the Greek variant 'anaphanentes' ('having been shown') rather than 'anaphanantes' ('having sighted').
notes.21:16: Vulgate 'adducentes secum ... Mnasonem' resolves a debated Greek dative construction by making Mnason the direct object accompanying the travelers ('bringing with them a certain Mnason') rather than a host awaiting them in Jerusalem.
notes.21:22: Vulgate 'utique oportet convenire multitudinem' ('Certainly the multitude must assemble') preserves the longer clause shared with the Byzantine tradition, which most modern critical Greek editions omit.
notes.21:28: Vulgate reads 'gentiles' ('Gentiles') where the Greek text has 'Hellenas' ('Greeks').
notes.21:38: Vulgate 'nonne tu es Aegyptius' frames the question positively ('Are you not the Egyptian...?') rather than as the negative inference of the Greek ('ouk ara,' 'So you are not the Egyptian...?').
notes.22:3: Vulgate distinctly reads 'juxta veritatem paternae legis' ('according to the truth of the ancestral law') and 'aemulator legis' ('zealous for the law'), where the Greek reads 'strictness' ('akribeian') and 'zealous for God' ('tou theou').
notes.22:12: Vulgate 'vir secundum legem' ('a man according to the law') omits the adjective 'devout' ('eulabes') present in the Greek text.
notes.22:24: Vulgate renders Greek 'mastixin anetazesthai' ('to be examined by scourging') with two explicit infinitives, 'flagellis caedi, et torqueri' ('to be beaten with whips and tortured'), echoed by 'torturi' in 22:29.
notes.22:30: Vulgate reads 'sacerdotes' ('the priests') rather than 'the chief priests' (Greek 'tous archiereis').
notes.23:9: The Clementine Vulgate reads simply "some of the Pharisees" (quidam pharisæorum) without mentioning scribes of the Pharisees' party, and ends the question at "or an angel?" without the longer Byzantine addition.
notes.23:25: This entire parenthetical verse explaining the tribune's fear of a false bribery charge is a distinctive Clementine Vulgate reading (reflecting the Western text tradition) absent from standard Greek editions, which instead place the opening clause of verse 26 here.
notes.23:30: The Vulgate reads "the ambush that they had prepared for him" (quas paraverant illi), omits "immediately," and concludes the letter with the concise instruction "to speak before you. Farewell."
notes.24:5: The Clementine Vulgate distinctively adds "of the sedition" (auctorem seditionis) before "of the sect of the Nazarenes," intensifying Tertullus's accusation of insurrection.
notes.24:8: Verse 7 (which in the longer tradition recounts the tribune Lysias taking Paul away by force) is absent from the main Latin text here, leaving the participle "ordering" (jubens) at the start of verse 8 syntactically attached to verse 6.
notes.24:14: Where the Greek reads "according to the Way which they call a sect" and "the ancestral God," the Clementine Vulgate distinctively reads "according to the sect that they call a heresy" (secundum sectam quam dicunt hæresim) and "the Father and my God" (Patri et Deo meo).
notes.24:17: The Clementine Vulgate adds "and vows" (et vota) alongside alms and offerings, a phrase absent from standard Greek texts.
notes.24:25: The Vulgate renders the Greek term for self-control specifically as castitate ("chastity").
notes.25:12: The Clementine Vulgate punctuates Caesarem appellasti? as a question ("Have you appealed to Caesar?"), whereas many modern editions of the Greek take it as a declarative statement.
notes.25:16: Vulgate damnare aliquem hominem ("to condemn any man") and ad abluenda crimina (literally "for washing away the charges") are distinctly Latin formulations where the Greek reads "hand over any man" and "concerning the charge."
notes.25:19: Latin superstitione ("superstition") renders Greek deisidaimonia ("religion" or "superstition") in its more dismissive Roman sense, reflecting Festus's viewpoint.
notes.25:24: The Clementine Vulgate reads Jerosolymis ("in Jerusalem") alone—without the Greek phrase "and here"—and uses two participles, petentes et acclamantes ("demanding and shouting out").
notes.26:5: Latin certissimam (literally "most certain" or "surest") renders Greek akribestaten ("strictest" or "most exact").
notes.26:19: Latin incredulus ("unbelieving" or "incredulous") translates Greek apeithes ("disobedient" or "unpersuaded"), preserving the Vulgate's focus on belief.
notes.26:23: Latin si ... si ("whether ... whether," mirroring Greek ei ... ei) introduces the two propositions, and passibilis literally means "capable of" or "subject to suffering."
notes.26:28: Latin In modico ("in a small measure" or "in a little") is famously debated—capable of meaning "in a short time," "with little effort," or "almost"—and is echoed in Paul's reply et in modico et in magno ("both in a small measure and in a great one") in verse 29.
notes.27:1: The Clementine Vulgate reads navigare eum ("that he should sail"), referring to Paul, whereas the Greek text has "that we should sail."
notes.27:5: The Clementine Vulgate reads Lystram ("Lystra") in Lycia, a Vulgate-distinct place name where the Greek text has Myra.
notes.27:8: The Clementine Vulgate names the harbor Boniportus ("Good Harbors") and the nearby city Thalassa, where most Greek manuscripts read Lasea.
notes.27:13: The Clementine Vulgate reads de Asson ("from Asson"), taking the Greek comparative adverb asson ("closer") as a proper place name.
notes.27:40: The Clementine Vulgate reads committebant se mari ("they committed themselves to the sea") after weighing the anchors, whereas the Greek text says they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea.
notes.27:44: The Clementine Vulgate adds the active verb ferebant ("they carried") for the rest of the passengers brought ashore on planks and ship debris.
notes.28:1: Latin barbari (literally 'barbarians') denotes non-Greek- and non-Latin-speaking local inhabitants rather than uncivilized people; the Vulgate also places this second sentence in verse 1 rather than verse 2.
notes.28:4: Latin ultio ('vengeance' or 'retribution') corresponds to Greek Dike ('Justice'), reflecting a pagan notion of personified divine retribution, and the Vulgate uses the present tense non sinit ('does not allow').
notes.28:11: Latin Castorum (literally 'of the Castors') is the idiomatic Latin plural for the twin deities Castor and Pollux, patron gods of sailors (corresponding to Greek Dioskouroi).
notes.28:25: The Vulgate reads patres nostros ('our fathers'), whereas many critical Greek editions read 'your fathers.'
notes.28:28: Verse 29 (reporting that the Jews departed debating among themselves) is absent from this Latin text, following the earliest Vulgate manuscripts.
